title: My Father works (John 5:10–30)
hook: healing on the sabbath: my Father is working still, and so am I

segments.voice: Yesterday, thirty-eight years by a pool, and a question: wilt thou be made whole? Your line was do you want to be well?

A man walks through Jerusalem with his rolled-up mat under his arm. It's the sabbath, the day of rest that Jewish law protects, and some of the religious leaders stop him: it is not lawful to carry your bed today. His answer is wonderfully human: the man who healed me told me to. Who was it? He doesn't know. He never got the name; Jesus had slipped away into the crowd. Later Jesus finds him in the temple, and the question of the sabbath reaches Jesus himself.

Jesus tells him: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee." The man goes and tells the leaders who healed him, and the argument begins. Remember, this is a debate among Jews about what keeping the sabbath means. Jesus answers in one sentence: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work." Hitherto means until now. Genesis says God rested on the seventh day. Yet the world keeps going on the sabbath: babies are born, rain falls, hearts beat. Jewish teachers asked the same question: how can God rest, when the world needs holding up every moment? Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of that time, answered that God never stops making and sustaining the world. Jesus stands inside that thought: if the Father is still at work, the Son works with him. His listeners hear the claim clearly: he is calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God. Then he describes how it works between them: "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do." Like an apprentice at a workbench, watching the master's hands and copying them. In Christian teaching, this passage is a key to who Jesus is: not a rival to God, but the Son doing what the Father does. And in Jesus's words it's a picture of a God who doesn't clock out, still at the work of healing and giving life.
screen: then, large: `MY FATHER WORKETH HITHERTO, AND I WORK.`

segments.voice: Notice what's working in you right now without any effort: your heart beating, your lungs filling, the ground holding you up. Then picture one small good work you could do, a message to someone lonely, a repair you've put off, carrying something for someone. If you pray, ask to see where God is already at work, and join in; if you don't, choose the work anyway.
Hitherto. It means until now, in Jesus's answer when he healed on the sabbath: My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.
Your line: god is still working. Even on the day of rest. Day six hundred six, done.

howItsDone: Christians read this passage as a teaching about Jesus as the Son of God; some also see in it a call to join in God's ongoing work of healing and care.

notes: Carrying a burden on the sabbath: cf. Jeremiah 17:21–22 and later rabbinic rules (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 lists carrying among the forbidden labors). Confirm.

The claim that Jewish teachers asked how God could rest while sustaining the world, with Philo as an example (Leg. All. 1.5–6) and later rabbinic discussion (e.g., Genesis Rabbah 11:10): confirm citations.

The script frames the sabbath argument as an intra-Jewish debate and avoids 'the Jews persecuted Jesus' (5:16); the KJV uses 'the Jews', which in John often means the Judean authorities. Confirm framing.
Index carry is lowercase 'god is still working'; kept exactly.
